demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Patient: Margaret, 68-year-old retired elementary school teacher, married. Seen for third session.

Margaret sits in the armchair with her hands folded in her lap, her posture rigid. She apologizes twice for the light in the room being too bright, though it is a gray, overcast afternoon. She has been coming to see me for three weeks, referred by her primary care doctor after a series of panic attacks sent her to the emergency room. She tells me she has not slept more than three hours a night since November.

She begins, as she always does, with the phone call. It is the only way she can enter the story.

It was a Tuesday. She was pulling a casserole out of the oven. Her husband, Frank, was in the garage, tinkering with his old fishing rods. The phone rang. It was her daughter, Sarah, but her voice was not Sarah’s voice. Sarah said, "Mom, it's Will." Will is her grandson. He was twenty-two. He had just graduated from trade school. He was driving home from a friend’s house. A drunk driver crossed the median.

Margaret remembers the sound she made. A sound she had never made before. A low, animal moan that seemed to come from somewhere behind her ribs. Frank ran in, and she dropped the phone. The casserole dish shattered on the tile floor. She remembers the glass, the smell of burnt cheese, the way her knees buckled.

That was eight months ago.

She has not been to the grocery store since. She cannot. The produce section is the worst. The bright lights, the colors, the people moving in slow, indifferent arcs. She feels a pressure behind her eyes, a tightness in her throat. She will stand in the cereal aisle, staring at boxes, and suddenly she is back in that moment—the hot oven, the ringing phone, the sound of her own voice. Once, she dropped a jar of pasta sauce. The shattering glass sent her into a full flashback. A store manager found her crouched between two shopping carts, sobbing, unable to speak.

She tells me she has stopped driving. She cannot trust her peripheral vision. She sees movement out of the corner of her eye and jerks the wheel, expecting a car to appear from nowhere. She nearly hit a mailbox last month. Frank drives her to these sessions. He waits in the car. She knows he is worried, but she cannot talk to him about it. He was there. He heard the phone ring too. She feels that she must protect him from her own mind.

Retirement was supposed to be a season of rest. She had taught second grade for thirty-four years. She loved the structure, the smell of crayons, the small, predictable rhythms of the school day. Now, the quiet of her house is a torture. The silence feels like a held breath. She fills it with television, but the news is full of sirens. She cannot watch crime dramas. She cannot listen to the radio in the car. A song that was playing that week—a pop song she used to hum while gardening—now triggers a wave of nausea.

At night, she does not sleep. She lies beside Frank and she watches the ceiling. She replays it. She wonders if Will had time to be scared. She wonders if he saw the headlights. She wonders if he thought of her. These questions are like a splinter she cannot remove. She knows, intellectually, that the accident was not her fault. But in the dark, her mind is a loop of guilt. She should have called him that night. She had thought about it. She wanted to ask if he had eaten. But she didn’t want to bother him.

She now feels a constant, low-grade dread. She scans every room for exits. She avoids crowds. She cancelled Christmas. She tells me she feels like a ghost in her own life. She is still here, but she is not present. She is stuck on that Tuesday, in the kitchen, waiting for a phone call that has already ended.
